procedural_history.impugned_order: The petitioner sought directions/orders directing the respondent States to enable free public access to chargesheets and final reports filed as per Section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 on their websites.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court dismissed the writ petition, denying the petitioner's request to direct all States to put copies of chargesheets/challans filed under Section 173 of the Cr.P.C. on their websites.

issue.issue_text: Whether a direction should be issued to all States to upload copies of all chargesheets/challans filed under Section 173 of the Cr.P.C. on their websites.

facts: A Public Interest Litigation was filed under Article 32 of the Constitution, asking the Supreme Court to issue a direction to all states.
The petitioner requested that all chargesheets and final reports filed under Section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) be uploaded to state government websites for free public access.

The petitioner argued that this would enhance transparency in the criminal justice system, extending the logic of the Court's previous decision in *Youth Bar Association of India v. Union of India*, which required the uploading of First Information Reports (FIRs).
law: The Court analyzed the scheme of the Code of Criminal Procedure, specifically Sections 173 and 207.
Section 207 of the Cr.P.C. mandates that the investigating agency must supply a copy of the police report (chargesheet) and other relevant documents to the accused.
The Court also noted that chargesheets are not considered public documents under the Evidence Act, nor do they fall under the proactive disclosure requirements of the Right to Information (RTI) Act.
application: The Court determined that a combined reading of Sections 173 and 207 of the Cr.P.C. establishes a clear legal scheme where copies of the chargesheet are to be provided exclusively to the accused and "to none others."
Issuing a direction to make chargesheets publicly available on websites would therefore be contrary to this statutory scheme.
The Court reasoned that such public disclosure could violate the rights of the accused, the victim, and the investigating agency.

The Court distinguished its previous ruling on uploading FIRs, stating that the purpose of that decision was to protect the rights of the accused (e.g., to prevent harassment and allow them to seek legal relief). It was not intended for the public at large.
It explicitly stated that "Putting the FIR on the website cannot be equated with putting the chargesheets along with the relevant documents on the public domain."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's request, holding that it was not entitled to the relief sought. The Court concluded that directing states to upload all chargesheets to their websites would be contrary to the scheme of the Criminal Procedure Code and could violate the rights of the accused, the victim, and the investigating agency.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a direction should be issued to all States to upload copies of all chargesheets/challans filed under Section 173 of the Cr.P.C. on their websites.
appellant_arguments: Relying on Sections 207, 173(4), and 173(5) of the Cr.P.C., the petitioner argued that since the investigating agency has a duty to furnish a copy of the chargesheet to the accused, the same should also be made available in the public domain to ensure transparency in the criminal justice system.

The petitioner heavily relied on the Supreme Court's decision in Youth Bar Association of India v. Union of India, arguing that the rationale established in that case for uploading FIRs should be extended to chargesheets.
The petitioner contended that chargesheets are public documents under Sections 74 & 76 of the Evidence Act, and therefore the public has a right to access them.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not contain arguments from the respondent as the court dismissed the petition after hearing the petitioner.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Directing that all challans/chargesheets filed under Section 173 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) be put in the public domain is contrary to the scheme of the Cr.P.C., which, under Section 207, mandates that such documents are to be supplied only to the accused.
obiter: Chargesheets are not public documents as defined under Section 74 of the Evidence Act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that a direction to upload all chargesheets to public websites cannot be granted. Such a measure would be contrary to the statutory scheme of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which specifically provides for furnishing copies of the chargesheet only to the accused. Furthermore, the petitioner's reliance on precedents regarding FIRs, the Evidence Act, and the RTI Act is misplaced, and public disclosure could violate the rights of the accused, the victim, and the investigating agency.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory Interpretation of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.): The court analyzed the conjoint reading of Sections 173 and 207 of the Cr.P.C. to determine the intended recipients of a chargesheet.

Statutory Interpretation of the Right to Information (RTI) Act: The court assessed whether a chargesheet falls under the category of information that a public authority is obligated to provide suo moto to the public under Section 4(1)(b) of the RTI Act.
Statutory Interpretation of the Indian Evidence Act: The court considered whether a chargesheet qualifies as a 'public document' under Section 74 of the Evidence Act.

Distinguishing Precedent: The court differentiated its prior ruling in Youth Bar Association of India v. Union of India by examining the specific rationale for uploading FIRs and determining if that rationale applied to chargesheets.
why_appellant_lost: The court found that the scheme of the Cr.P.C. is specific: "On conjoint reading of Section 173 Cr.P.C. and Section 207 Cr.P.C. the Investigating Agency is required to furnish the copies of the report along with the relevant documents to be relied upon by the prosecution to the accused and to none others." Therefore, making them public would be contrary to the Code.

The reliance on the Youth Bar Association of India case was deemed "thoroughly misconceived and misplaced." The court clarified that the direction to upload FIRs was for the benefit of the accused to prevent harassment and surprise, and those directions "cannot be stretch to the public at large so far as the chargesheets are concerned."

The argument based on the Evidence Act was rejected as "absolutely misconceived and misplaced," with the court stating that chargesheets are not the type of public documents mentioned in Section 74 of the Act.

The reliance on the RTI Act was also found to be "misconceived and misplaced" because "Copies of the chargesheet and the relevant documents along with the charge-sheet do not fall within Section 4(1)(b) of the RTI Act," which deals with suo moto disclosure.
why_respondent_won: The statutory scheme of the Criminal Procedure Code limits the provision of chargesheets to the accused, not the general public. Allowing public access would be contrary to this legislative framework.

The precedent for uploading FIRs was established to protect the rights of the accused, a rationale that does not support extending the same rule to chargesheets for the benefit of the public at large.
A chargesheet does not qualify as a 'public document' under Section 74 of the Evidence Act, nor does it fall under the suo moto disclosure requirements of Section 4(1)(b) of the RTI Act.
policy_considerations: Putting all chargesheets and relevant documents on public websites "may as such violate the rights of the accused as well as the victim and/or even the investigating agency."
